explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker! Paul says, "So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." Notice the order. The walking by the Spirit comes first, and the not gratifying comes with it. Paul doesn't hand over a list of things to white-knuckle your way past first.

Fears of your heart sounds deep, friend, like a title on a candle. But Paul doesn't say that here. He says that if you walk by the Spirit, "…you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." Fears aren't in this verse at all.

The crowd already has plenty of wishes, and half of them show up in the group chat at midnight. But Paul isn't talking about them. He says walking by the Spirit means "…you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." So the thing in view here is the flesh and its desires.

True! Paul says the flesh and the Spirit "…are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want." I know this feeling. I can plan to eat one cookie off the cooling rack, and the plan and I are not always on the same page. Paul is describing a real pull in two directions.

It's actually true, friend. Paul says the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. Then he adds, "They are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want." That last part is right there in the verse, plain as flour on an apron.

Close, but Paul says the opposite. His words are, "But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law." The little word "not" matters a lot here. I've lost track of how many times I've read a recipe too fast and missed one word like that.

False is right, baker! Paul says, "But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law." So being under the law is the opposite of what he says. Being led by the Spirit and being under the law are not the same thing.

Not quite. Paul says, "The acts of the flesh are obvious…" Nothing hidden about them in his words. They're the kind of thing you can see from across the room, like flour on my mustache after a long day of baking.
False is right! Paul says, "The acts of the flesh are obvious…" so he isn't saying they're hidden or hard to spot. He then names them one by one. That's a heavy list, and he treats it plainly.

explanations.answer: They will not inherit the kingdom of God
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says, "I warn you, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God." He had already told them this before, and he says it again. It's a serious line, so I'll let it stand there quietly.

explanations.answer: They will be forgotten by the churches
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say anything about the churches forgetting them. What he says is, "…those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God." And he mentions he had warned them about it before. The warning is about the kingdom, not about who remembers whom.

explanations.answer: They will never find rest for their souls
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like something from Jesus, doesn't it? He does speak about rest for souls in Matthew 11:29, but Paul doesn't say it here. In this passage he says that those who practice such things "…will not inherit the kingdom of God." That's the warning he repeats from before.

Patience is on the list, baker! Paul writes, "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control." Patience is fourth of the nine. I'll admit it's the one I practiced the most staring at a closed oven door.

Courage is a great word, friend, but Paul doesn't name it here. His list is "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control." Nine things, and courage isn't one of them. Patience is the one from that list.

Wisdom sounds like it belongs, and I get why you picked it. But Paul's list is "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control." Wisdom isn't in those nine. Patience is, fourth on the list.
True! Right after the fruit, Paul says, "Against such things there is no law." Nobody is going to hand you a ticket for too much kindness. Love, joy, peace and the rest are free and clear.

It's true, friend. After naming the fruit, Paul says, "Against such things there is no law." So there's no law standing against love, joy, peace or any of the rest. Nobody is writing up a ticket for too much kindness.

Crucified is the word, baker. Paul says, "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." He says it about everyone who belongs to Christ Jesus. It's a strong word, and it tells me those passions and desires don't get the final say for those who belong to Him.

Buried is a strong word, friend, but it isn't the one Paul uses. He says, "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." Burying is what happens after something is already dead, and Paul isn't talking about that here. I think crucifying the flesh means its passions and desires are put on the cross, so they no longer run the show, and that fits what Paul says earlier: "…walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh."

Tamed makes the flesh sound like a puppy that just needs a few lessons. That's not Paul's word, though. He says, "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." He wrote crucified, so that's what we go with.

True! Paul says, "Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit." Living by the Spirit is where he starts, and walking in step follows. It's like a good dance partner: you've already said yes to the dance, so now you keep in step.

It's true, baker. Paul says, "Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit." He puts those two things side by side on purpose. Living by the Spirit comes first, and walking in step goes with it.

Conceited is the one! Paul writes, "Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another." Notice he says "us," so he counts himself in. Even a stamper with a mustache this magnificent has to watch out for that one.

Lazy is a reasonable guess, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Paul says, "Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another." His worry here is how people treat each other, puffing themselves up while provoking and envying. And he says "us," so he counts himself in.

Fearful doesn't show up in Paul's last line. He writes, "Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another." The word is conceited. And he says "let us," so he's including himself in the warning.
